records.topic: WP AER 48 split design and pressure steps
records.claim: Air spring lives in the left leg in its own internal chamber with a single fill valve; damping cartridge is in the right leg. WP advises changing pressure in small steps and checking pressure regularly with its gauge-equipped pump.
records.mechanism: Single 34 mm air chamber with bypass for pressure compensation and integrated hydro-top; separate air chamber means fork holds air even if main seal fails.
records.direction: Adjust air pressure in 0.2 bar increments; check pressure regularly
records.numbers: 0.2 bar adjustment increment; 34 mm air chamber and 34 mm damping cartridge (WP AER 48)
records.quote: will hold air, even when the fork seal fails

records.topic: Air spring tuned to rider weight without opening fork
records.claim: WP positions the air spring as the way to match fork to rider weight and track features without disassembly.
records.direction: Use air pressure, not spring swaps, to match rider weight

components: WP XACT PRO 7448 AER air fork

records.claim: WP's Cone Valve replaces the shim stack with a conical valve; WP says this removes damping loss from bent shims, keeps pressure drop small once the valve opens, and reduces harshness even with a firmer setup.
records.mechanism: Removing a sealing surface means only a minimal pressure drop after opening; conical valve reduces oil-flow turbulence and initial breakaway force.
records.conditions: Cone-valve (Pro Components) forks only, not standard OEM XACT

records.claim: WP's closed cartridge isolates a smaller oil volume and is internally pressurised, which WP says prevents cavitation and damping loss on demanding tracks.
records.mechanism: Pressurised separated oil volume avoids cavitation

components: WP XACT PRO 7448 AER air fork

records.claim: XACT PRO 7448 uses a two-chamber AER air spring whose pressure is adjusted to change fork response; the 2019 release says the two separate chambers give setup options for initial response.
records.mechanism: Second chamber acts on the initial part of the stroke
records.conditions: Pro Components air fork, not the standard OEM XACT air fork
records.numbers: Travel 11.97 in; inner tube 1.89 in; length 37.2 in (XACT PRO 7448 product page)

records.topic: Standard XACT Air has no separate balance chamber; Pro Air does
records.claim: Per MXA (not WP): OEM XACT Air has one Schrader valve and transfers pressure from the collapsing side to act as a negative spring against top-out; XACT Pro Air has separate main and balance chambers, and changing the pressure difference alters ride height, plushness and fork length.
records.mechanism: Main chamber pushes fork down, balance chamber pushes it back up to prevent topping; ratio is the tuning lever.
records.conditions: Secondary source; confirm against WP documentation
records.direction: On Pro Air, change main/balance difference to change ride height and initial feel

records.topic: SUPERTRAX / TRAX bypass on XACT PRO shocks
records.claim: A unit in the lower shock mount senses when the rear wheel loses ground contact and opens an oil bypass so the wheel returns to the ground faster; WP claims less packing over repeated bumps and more rear grip.
records.mechanism: SUPERTRAX senses spring speed in rebound and activates bypass; TXN adjuster sets the linked rebound behaviour.
records.conditions: Only on Pro Components shocks with TRAX/SUPERTRAX
records.direction: Use TXN adjuster to add rebound control or sensitivity as terrain changes

records.claim: XACT PRO 8950 offers spring preload, high- and low-speed compression, high- and low-speed rebound, plus the TXN rebound adjuster.
records.numbers: 50 mm piston, 18 mm rod, 138 mm stroke, 477 mm length, 4335 g (KTM 2025 300 XC-W TPI fitment page)

records.topic: WP: setup data from authorized centers
records.claim: WP's 2023 XACT PRO release gives no settings and sends owners to a WP Authorized Center for setup; all fork settings are externally adjustable.

Measure unloaded (L1), then with rider on pegs push down ~15 mm and let rise slowly (L2), lift ~15 mm and let settle slowly (L3); sag = L1 minus the average of L2 and L3. Rider stands on pegs for dirt bikes and balances without gripping with knees or leaning on bars.
records.mechanism: Averaging cancels friction (stiction) in seals and linkage.
records.conditions: Both wheels same height off ground for L1
records.numbers: 15 mm (1/2 in) push/lift; method consistent within 1 mm

records.topic: Stiction zone as linkage health check
records.claim: The gap between the push-down and lift-up sag readings is the stiction zone; Race Tech says if it exceeds a few millimetres the linkage needs attention.
records.mechanism: Friction in linkage bearings/seals holds the bike at different heights
records.direction: Service/grease linkage if stiction zone is large
records.numbers: More than 4 to 5 mm difference indicates linkage needs attention

records.claim: 1995 Race Tech article: rear linkage friction difference under ~3 mm is good, over ~10 mm is bad; forks under ~15 mm good, some measured over 50 mm.
records.numbers: Rear <3 mm good, >10 mm bad; front <15 mm good, some >50 mm

components: rear shock, full-size and mini dirt bikes

records.claim: Race Tech gives typical dirt-bike rider sag as about a third of travel, with ranges for full-size and mini bikes; says there is no single correct number and riders may prefer a bit more or less.
records.direction: Too much sag -> add preload; too little -> remove preload
records.numbers: 30-33% of travel; full-size 95-110 mm; 80cc 85-105 mm; 50-65cc 55-75 mm
records.quote: If you have too much Sag you need more preload.

records.claim: Industry spring-rate tolerance is about ±5%, so nominally different springs can overlap; Race Tech claims tighter tolerances on its own springs.
records.numbers: ±5% industry tolerance

records.topic: Teknik rear sag table by bike class
records.claim: Teknik gives rear rider and static sag targets per class; rear static sag about a third of stroke is a starting point; KTM PDS is very sensitive to rear height.
records.numbers: MX/enduro rear static 30 ±8 mm, rider 100 +8/-3 mm; KTM PDS rider 110 +8/-5 (start 105, practical 90-110 mm); 80/85 rider 85 ±3 mm (KTM 85 near 100 mm); 50/65 rider 65 ±5 mm

records.claim: Teknik also sets fork sag targets, static and rider.
records.numbers: 125/250/450 MX & enduro fork static 30 ±10 mm, rider 50 ±10 mm; 80/85 static 15 ±5, rider 40 ±5; 50/65 static 15 ±5, rider 30 ±5

records.topic: Reading spring rate from static vs rider sag
records.claim: With static sag correct: rider sag below minimum means spring too firm, above maximum means spring too soft. Lighter springs need more preload, heavier less; a firmer spring can feel more compliant early because it needs less preload.
records.mechanism: Excess preload on a soft spring makes the start of stroke harsh.
records.direction: Change spring when preload alone cannot bring both sag numbers into range

records.topic: Fork preload range and usable spring options
records.claim: Fork preload normally sits in a small range; too much preload on very soft fork springs gives harsh feel and poor grip. Typically 2-3 usable fork rates and 3 usable shock rates exist per rider. Heavier springs suit sand, mud, pro four-strokes and big jumpers. OEM springs lose free length over time.
records.direction: Record preload in mm when changing rates to keep geometry similar; recheck sag if handling changes over time
records.numbers: Fork preload normally 3-14 mm

records.topic: Release fork stiction before tightening pinch bolts
records.claim: Tighten fork pinch bolts only after compressing the forks several times to neutralise binding.

On shocks, LSC is the slotted screw on the reservoir top, HSC the larger hex on the same adjuster, rebound the slotted screw at the bottom. Closed-cartridge forks: compression at top, rebound at base; open-cartridge: reversed. Count all settings out from fully clockwise (hard), change one adjuster at a time, do not overtighten.

components: forks and shocks without maker baseline

records.claim: Generic starting points when no spec exists: forks with many clicks start at 10/10; forks without clicks 1.5 turns out; forks with few clicks midway; shock 1 turn out HSC, 10 LSC, 10 rebound. Clickers change damping rate but not the valving, which must suit the application.
records.conditions: Use only when manufacturer baseline unavailable
records.numbers: Forks >20 clicks: 10 comp, 10 reb; no clicks: 1.5 turns out; shock: HSC 1 turn out, LSC 10, rebound 10

records.claim: Measure fork height from bottom of lower clamp to tube end. Sliding forks up puts more weight on the front and quickens turning; lowering them reduces steering angle and steadies a front that falls into corners. Change in small steps.
records.mechanism: Changes rake/trail and front weight bias
records.direction: Up for turning, down for stability
records.numbers: One clamp line about 3 mm; typical change about 5 mm

records.topic: Fork oil level controls late stroke
records.claim: Raising fork oil level firms the late stroke (bottoming resistance); lowering softens late stroke. Adjust in small steps when fixing harsh bottoming. In twin-chamber forks the spring perch damps more as oil rises.
records.mechanism: Less air volume means air gap becomes more progressive
records.conditions: Measured with top nut off, fork fully compressed, no spring/preload washer
records.direction: Bottoming: raise oil; harsh deep in stroke but fine on small bumps: lower oil
records.numbers: 5 mm increments; chart range 140-240 mm

records.claim: Front falls into turns (esp. sand): more compression, stiffer springs, lower forks ~5 mm. Unstable on brakes: raise oil, stiffer springs, more compression. Harsh, not using travel, poor grip in bumpy turns: less compression, softer springs. Bottoms but fine on small bumps: raise oil. Fine small bumps but harsh late: lower oil. Rides low and soft early but no bottoming: raise oil or softer springs, less compression, less preload, clean seals. Good on first bump, harsh after several: less rebound. Rebounds fast with poor grip: more rebound, less preload. Headshake: check spring rate, reduce rebound, check steering head bearings.
records.numbers: lower forks ~5 mm

records.claim: Teknik's sequence for a bike that won't turn: more rear preload (keeping static sag at least 15 mm), slide forks up 5 mm, more rear LSC, adjust fork compression/rebound two clicks at a time, then reduce fork preload or soften springs as last resort; check fork centring.
records.numbers: Rear static sag ≥15 mm; forks up 5 mm; 2-click steps

records.claim: Rear won't hook up: recheck sag, less rebound, check axle position/chain length, less HSC on rocks/roots. Can't handle whoops: more compression (esp. HSC) and more rebound without packing. Rear bottoms: more compression, add preload (not beyond 5 mm under recommended rider sag), less rebound. Kick under power: if packing soften rebound, if bottoming stiffen compression or add preload.
records.numbers: Preload no more than 5 mm below recommended rider sag

records.claim: On acceleration bumps, if the rear breaks up soften LSC, else soften rebound two clicks. Add compression only until the shock bottoms on the biggest obstacle. On braking bumps soften rebound until the rear hops, then firm until it stops. Rear bouncing after landings: more rebound; packing in whoops: less rebound.
records.numbers: 2-click steps

records.topic: Which terrain tests which damping circuit
records.claim: Low-speed rebound: test on small bumps/washboard/off-camber; aim to stop bouncing while letting wheel extend. High-speed rebound: medium/large rolling bumps, fast downhills; stop kicking without packing. Low-speed compression: small/medium bumps, sand whoops, gullies; prevent bottoming without skipping under braking. High-speed compression: big square edges and jumps; limit bottoming without harshness.

Hardpack: soften compression both ends. Sand: add rebound first, then compression as track roughens; clickers may end near maximum unless revalved for sand. Supercross: stiffen compression, possibly raise oil or stiffer springs.
records.numbers: Sand: +1-2 clicks rebound, then +1-4 clicks compression; SX: +2-6 clicks compression

records.claim: Record clickers, spring rates, preload, oil level, fork height and tyre pressures per track to be able to return to a known baseline.

records.topic: Design rider weight of stock bikes
records.claim: Stock MX springs are aimed at about a 75 kg rider and enduro at about 85 kg, including kit; heavier riders should respring and revalve.
records.conditions: Magazine article distributed by Teknik; consistent with Teknik guide's 75 kg target
records.numbers: MX 75 kg; enduro 85 kg

records.topic: Clicker usable range and feel threshold
records.claim: Clickers act like taps on an orifice. A typical clicker has around 24 clicks but the usable range is roughly 4-20 out; about two clicks is the smallest change most riders feel on good suspension. Start front rebound, then front compression, then rear.
records.mechanism: Adjuster needle restricts a bleed orifice
records.numbers: ~24 clicks total; usable 4-20 out; 2 clicks to feel

records.claim: Fork rebound: bars push back on lipped take-off = too soft (wind in); no front grip in flat turns = too hard (wind out). Fork compression: clunk on landings = too soft; front runs wide in fast corners = too hard. Shock rebound: kicks every whoop = too soft; kicks once at end of braking bumps = too hard. Shock compression: pegs scrape on landings = too soft; rear swaps in whoops under power = too hard.

records.topic: Why KYB PSF uses a balance spring
records.claim: Air alone is very soft at the start and very progressive late; KYB added a light coil balance spring to firm the initial stroke and make it more linear. In PSF1/PSF2 the coil also serves as the rebound top-out bumper. Heavier riders need stiffer balance springs and higher pressure.
records.mechanism: Halving gas volume doubles pressure: at half travel pressure doubles, at three-quarters it doubles again.

components: WP AER 48 (2016+) with Race Tech spring conversion

records.claim: Race Tech says air-to-coil conversion improves ride quality, removes blowout risk and ongoing air maintenance. Depressurise all chambers before removing the cap; set coil preload small; no bleeding needed after fill.
records.numbers: Damping-leg USF-05 oil: 525 cc MX, 575 cc SX, 500 cc off-road; preload 3-5 mm

records.topic: Fork bushings and air fork service cautions

components: 2015 KYB single-chamber air fork with balance spring

records.claim: Release air pressure before disassembly; keep left/right leg parts separate (compression on left cap, rebound on right); inspect bushings and tube for wear and straightness; bushings may be damaged on removal, so have spares.
records.numbers: Do not heat cartridge thread over 350 °F

records.topic: What a compression Gold Valve kit changes

components: Race Tech compression Gold Valve (bolt type) in KYB/Showa cartridges

records.claim: Gold Valve replaces the compression piston and shim stack with a stack specified per rider on Race Tech's DVS sheet; stacks are single-stage (low/high speed) or two-stage (with crossover); bleed hole only if specified.
records.mechanism: Two-stage stack uses a smaller crossover shim between low- and high-speed sections

records.topic: Bottom-out bumper effective range and wear items
records.claim: Race Tech notes bottom-out bumpers degrade and should be replaced; worn coating on 2017+ Showa 14 mm damping-rod forks causes internal cartridge seal leaks; bladders wear out and are replaceable.
rider_words: bottoms harder than it used to
records.numbers: Bumpers typically effective over 25-33% of travel

records.topic: KYB factory kit fork and shock design
records.claim: KYB factory fork is an air-oil separated closed cartridge with DLC inner tubes; an added mid-speed valve widens the adjustment range. Factory shock has HSC, LSC, rebound and preload adjust, Kashima body and DLC shaft, and an Xtrig preload adjuster.

records.topic: Öhlins TTX Flow MX shock architecture

components: Öhlins TTX Flow MX & Enduro shock (YA 1892, HO 2093, KT 1984, KT 2082)

records.claim: TTX Flow MX shock is twin-tube with high-pressure gas piggyback reservoir, one compression (C1 Flow) and one rebound (R1 Flow) adjuster; some versions (Q1) add a second piston for progressive damping. Supplied without spring; spring chosen by rider weight from the mounting instructions.
records.numbers: 46 mm piston; KT 2082: 415 mm length, 100 mm stroke; spring series 06310/06320/06451/06452 depending on model

components: Öhlins RXF48 fork + TTX MX shock

records.claim: Öhlins order: choose spring rates, set sag and check free sag, set fork preload and fluid volume, ride and analyse position (balance) problems, then fine-tune with clickers. If free sag is near the limit at nominal sag, change spring rate.
records.numbers: Example 108 mm sag and 42 mm free sag; +5 mm sag suggested as first step for traction

records.topic: Öhlins RXF48 fluid volume = air spring tuning
records.claim: More fluid reduces air volume and adds progressive force mainly mid to end stroke: better bottoming resistance but can harshen small bumps; less fluid does the opposite.
records.numbers: 10 ml steps

records.claim: Öhlins says rear spring rate mainly affects the end of the stroke while front spring rate mainly affects mid-stroke; rear spring by rider weight in gear, front by bike plus rider weight in gear.

records.topic: Öhlins clicker convention and preload rules
records.claim: Turn adjusters gently to fully closed (0) and count clicks out; clockwise adds damping. Preload below zero leaves springs loose when the wheel is unloaded; preload washers must go below the spring or they restrict flow and can break the fork.
records.numbers: Example preload 10 mm (445 - 300 - 135)

records.claim: Front bottoms on big jumps: softer rear spring/shift weight rearward, add fork fluid. Rear bottoms on big jumps: harder rear spring, close HSC, remove fork fluid. Turns wide: add rear preload, raise forks in clamps, remove fluid, softer springs. Turns in too tight: remove rear preload, push forks down.

Bleed the fork's breather plugs regularly; clean scrapers and oil the tube; avoid brake cleaner. Schedule covers fluid change, seals/scrapers, cartridge service and bushings for the fork, and shock service, piston band and piston for the shock, at every-race / 20 / 40 / 60 hour stages (task-to-interval mapping not reliable in the text extraction).
records.numbers: Interval columns: every race, 20 h, 40 h, 60 h; cartridge shaft end 18 Nm; top cap max 10 Nm

records.claim: A holeshot device holds the fork compressed to lower the front, shifting load rearward to reduce wheelies and wheelspin; it releases in the first turn when braking compresses the fork further. Check it does not conflict with the fork's compression system.
records.quote: releases in the first turn when the brakes are pulled and the bike compresses

disagreements.topic: Linkage/fork stiction threshold in sag readings

positions.says: More than 4-5 mm difference means the linkage needs attention
Rear under ~3 mm good, over ~10 mm bad; forks under 15 mm good

disagreements.topic: Rear rider sag on full-size MX bikes

positions.says: Lists both 'static sag below minimum' and 'static sag above maximum' (with rider sag correct) as spring too soft, which looks internally inconsistent; conventional reading is little free sag = spring too soft, excess free sag = spring too stiff
If free sag is near recommended limits at nominal sag, change spring rate (no direction given in extraction)
Raise fork oil level in 5 mm steps (and increase compression)
Add fork fluid in 10 ml steps, and also look at rear spring/weight balance first
3-5 mm for its AER48 coil conversion
Example 10 mm; below 0 mm is wrong

disagreements.topic: WP air-fork weight saving and chamber layout claims vary between releases

positions.says: AER 48 saves about 3 lb; single 34 mm chamber with bypass
XACT PRO AER saves up to 1 kg; two separate chambers
Air spring saves 2.2 lb vs steel spring
XACT Air about 3.6 lb lighter than XACT Spring (magazine figure)

disagreements.topic: Does Cone Valve eliminate or reduce shims

positions.says: Reduces the number of damping shims
Replaces the mid-valve shim stack with a tapered cone held by a coil spring; three optional cones
